Verification & Evidence ​

An agent reporting success is a claim, not a result. Verification is the layer that decides whether a task may reach done — and it deliberately does not ask the agent that did the work.

Two levels of evidence exist, strongest first:

  • command — a shell command actually ran and exited zero. Mechanical, unfakeable.
  • model — an independent verifier reads only {task, criteria, reported output} and rules on it. It never shares the doer's session, so it cannot inherit the doer's belief that it succeeded.

The honest limit, stated in the source itself: a model verifier judges what the doer reported. If the doer misrepresents its work and no criterion names a checkable artifact, the gate catches nothing. That is why the plan schema pushes for observable criteria — the gate is only as strong as the artifacts it can point at.

Acceptance criteria ​

acceptanceCriteria is required on every plan item (min(1), max(5) in the set_plan / amend_plan schema). Each one must be an observable condition: a file that must exist, a command that must pass, a count, an output that must contain a specific thing. The schema explicitly rejects "it is good", and instructs that criteria be scoped to the symptom in the brief rather than an exhaustive survey of the surrounding subsystem.

Criteria are also shown to the doer in its brief, in both execution modes. Verifying work against criteria the agent never saw fails correct work for not answering a question it was never asked.

A task with no non-empty criterion is not passed — it is recorded as skipped, with the reason No acceptance criteria to check against. The absence of a contract stays visible rather than being silently rewarded.

Criteria are matched by a normalized key: case, internal whitespace, and trailing .!;: are not meaningful differences.

Checks: mechanical, judged by exit code ​

A TaskCheck is a shell command whose exit code decides. Output is captured for the report but never parsed — "the command printed the word success" is exactly the soft evidence checks exist to replace.

ts
{ cmd: 'npx tsc --noEmit', expectExit: 0, criterion: 'the project typechecks' }
FieldMeaning
cmdShell command, max 500 chars (MAX_CHECK_CMD_CHARS)
expectExitExit code that means passed. Defaults to 0
criterionThe exact acceptance-criterion text this check proves
trustedNot settable from the plan schema — see below

expectExit is what lets a check assert an absence: echo new-value | grep -q old-value with expectExit: 1 passes precisely when the old value is gone.

At most MAX_TASK_CHECKS (3) checks run per task. Empty commands, over-long commands, and unsafe commands are dropped before execution, and the remainder is sliced to 3.

Pass and fail are not symmetric ​

  • A failing check fails the task outright, no matter who wrote it. A failing check is real evidence of failure regardless of its author.
  • A passing check does not complete the task. The plan author writes both the criteria and the checks, so {cmd: "true", criterion: "<copy of a real criterion>"} would otherwise certify the task. Only a trusted check — one from a source the run did not author — may mark a criterion proven, and trusted is not exposed in the plan schema at all.

A passing check therefore proves the criterion it names, and only when trusted. Everything else still goes to the verifier. So a model-authored check can only ever make the gate stricter, never weaker.

What a check is allowed to run ​

Checks are authored by a model and executed as real shell commands against a real repo, and — unlike every other model-initiated command — they never pass through the worker permission gate. unsafeCheckReason is that gate instead, and it is an allow-list, because the denylist it replaced let through git reset --hard HEAD~1, echo broken > src/index.ts, and node -e.

Allowed programs (inspection tools only):

test [ true false exit echo printf
ls cat head tail wc stat file find basename dirname realpath
grep egrep fgrep rg diff cmp sort uniq cut tr awk sed jq
npm npx pnpm yarn node python python3 git

Refused on top of that:

RefusedWhy
Command substitution — $(…), backticks, ${…}The command text would never have been reviewed
Any redirection (>, >>) or teeA check asserts; it does not write
A program invoked by path (/bin/sh -c …)Rejection is by basename, so paths are refused outright
node/python/python3 with -e, -c, --eval, --command, --printTurns an allowed program into an arbitrary interpreter
sed -iIn-place editing is a write
Any git subcommand outside status log show diff rev-parse ls-files ls-tree cat-file branch describe shortlog blame grep configreset, checkout, clean, push can destroy the work under verification

Every segment of a pipeline is validated, not just the first — echo x \| node -e … is refused on the second segment. Pipes and ; stay allowed, because honest checks use them.

An unsafe check is dropped, not run. Dropping fails open to the model verifier: the criterion it claimed simply stays unproven, so removing a check can never turn into an easier pass. set_plan rejects these up front too, so this is the second line rather than the only one.

Checks run under bash -c (never a login shell, which could re-export the stripped credentials), with a 60-second timeout, in the run's own workspace, and with an environment derived from the worker env minus anything whose name looks like a credential (KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, CREDENTIAL, AUTH, SESSION).

A check that cannot even start is a failed check, not a crashed run.

Proofs: a closed, deterministic vocabulary ​

Where a shell command is too much rope, a TaskProof is evaluated by the engine itself — read-only, and bound to one exact criterion.

kindFieldsPasses when
fileExistspathThe path resolves inside the workspace and is a regular, non-symlink file
assetCountminCount, extensionAt least minCount (min 1) run assets exist, optionally filtered by extension suffix

path must be relative and must resolve — after realpath — inside the workspace root; anything absolute, ~-prefixed, or escaping the root is refused. Suffix/glob matching is deliberately unsupported so a proof cannot accidentally cover more than it names. A plan may carry at most 5 proofs.

Because the vocabulary is closed and the engine evaluates it, a proof may certify the criterion it names outright. A failed proof fails the task immediately with by: 'evidence', failureKind: 'work_missing', and the reason Engine evidence is missing for: … — the verifier is never consulted.

Proofs are described to the doer in its brief, with the note that the engine will collect them directly and it should reference them concisely rather than pasting raw files or logs.

Evidence the engine collects for itself ​

Workers may describe their work; they cannot author these.

PieceContents
EvidenceArtifactpath, kind (run-asset | workspace-file), size, sha256
EvidenceCommandcmd, exitCode, ok, durationMs, output tail, cached
EvidenceChangesbranch, base, commits (max 20), per-file status/additions/deletions (max 50), totals

EvidenceChanges is read straight off git for work-mode project tasks. It is the one piece of evidence a repo task always has and nobody has to ask for: proofs and checks are authored when the plan is frozen — before the work exists — so they cannot name a file the fix invents. The diff can, because it is read afterwards.

base is resolved as the branch's nearest ancestor, tried across the caller's hint plus staging, develop, main, master (local and origin/), keeping only genuine ancestors and picking the one with the fewest commits between it and the branch. A mis-resolved base does not fail loudly — a three-dot diff silently walks back to a distant merge-base and attributes another branch's entire divergence to this run.

The whole set is packaged as a TaskEvidenceManifest, which also carries reportSha256, provenCriteria, and failedCriteria.

The empty manifest ​

A manifest is always built, so "there is a manifest" is not the same question as "the engine collected anything". When nothing was collected, the verifier is told exactly that:

NONE — this task declared no checks or proofs, so the engine had nothing to collect. That is a fact about the PLAN, not about the work.

Pasting empty artifacts: [] / commands: [] arrays under an "authoritative" heading made a gate conclude the engine had looked and found nothing. It had not looked.

The verifier and its verdicts ​

The verifier is a fresh sub-agent with no tools, no session resume, and a system prompt that states it did not do the work and has no stake in it. It runs on the cheap tier at low effort with a thinking budget of 1024 tokens (the API minimum for extended thinking — below that the provider rejects the call outright and the gate silently disables itself). Its whole input is the task, the still-open criteria, the engine evidence section, and the doer's report clipped to 60,000 characters from both ends, because a report ends with its exit codes and citations.

Its reply contract is trivial on purpose: first token PASS or FAIL, then one sentence. Anything unparseable is treated as a FAIL — an ambiguous verdict must never read as permission to proceed. The reason is clipped to 800 characters, keeping the end.

The verdict lands on the task as TaskVerification:

FieldValues
statuspassed | failed | skipped
bycommand | evidence | model | none
reasonOne sentence, shown to the operator and replayed on retry
failureKindwork_missing | semantic_failure | proof_missing | environment_failure | provider_failure
atTimestamp

failureKind exists so a retry can be routed. work_missing means an artifact or check is actually absent or failed; semantic_failure is judged quality; proof_missing means the work may exist but the available report cannot establish it.

Every verdict — passes included — appends to the run-level verificationLog as a TaskVerificationRecord, which denormalises the task text and records the attempt, plan version, and the gate's own token spend. It lives outside the checklist, so no plan amendment can erase it.

When the gate cannot run ​

VerifyDecision is a union of two shapes, not two statuses: "the work is wrong" and "the gate could not run" are different events. A provider outage used to be recorded as a FAIL, which failed finished work and charged it an attempt it never used.

An unavailable decision that is transient is retried up to VERIFY_RETRIES (2) times with backoff, each try billed to the run's ledger. If it still cannot run, the task is set to blocked, not failed: the verdict is recorded as skipped with failureKind: provider_failure or environment_failure, the agent's report is kept, and the attempt is refunded.

A failed verdict whose input was truncated is also refunded — a task must never burn its budget on the size of its own report.

On failure, the doer's report stays in evidence and the verdict travels in verification.reason. The reason stands in only when there is no report at all.

The order of the gate ​

For a settled task, in this order:

  1. Run the task's usable checks (in the run's worktree, or under the repo lock with the run branch checked out when there is no worktree) and collect the evidence manifest.
  2. Any failed proof → task failed, by: 'evidence'.
  3. Any failed check → task failed, by: 'command'.
  4. Compute the criteria still unproven by trusted checks and proofs. If none remain → task done without a model call.
  5. Otherwise, run the model verifier on only the unproven criteria; the already-proven ones are shown as settled with an instruction not to re-judge them.
  6. passed → done. failed → failed. unavailable → blocked and refunded.

A project's own verify: policy command is passed to the verifier as context only, labelled a regression signal. It proves the build still compiles and the suite still passes; it says nothing about this task's criteria. Treating it as a pass meant every work task on such a repo self-certified with nothing ever reading its criteria.

finish_run refuses to close an unverified run ​

finish_run applies two separate gates. It refuses when any plan step is still open, and — when verification is active for the run — it refuses again if any step reached done without a passing verification:

Not finishing: 2 steps completed without passing verification:
- …
Re-delegate them so their acceptance criteria are actually checked.

A task marked done that nothing verified is precisely the claim this layer exists to stop accepting.

Which runs verify ​

ts
verificationEnabled(executionMode) === executionMode === 'guided'
  || getSystemSettings().verifyTasks === true

Guided runs always verify — the gate is the point of the mode. Autonomous runs opt in via Settings (verifyTasks, default false). See Modes & Permissions.

On the settle path that runs with no verifier, the report is at least read rather than stamped done unread. reportSelfAssessment is deliberately conservative: a report that leads with BLOCKED (however punctuated) settles as blocked, and a report containing ✗ marks and no ✓ marks settles as failed or blocked. A mixed ✓/✗ report still settles as done — judging partial results is the verifier's job.

Attempt budgets and escalation ​

Attempts are counted per checklist task. setTaskState(…, 'running') increments; an approval continuing the same piece of work does not increment again.

SettingDefaultMeaning
maxTaskAttempts3Attempts on one task before it must be escalated
maxSameTaskDispatches3Dispatches of the same (target, task) before the runtime refuses
maxDelegationFails3Consecutive failures for one target before it leaves rotation
attemptBudget (per task)—Per-task override, clamped to the configured maximum

A task at or past its budget is not retried. It is set to blocked with a terminal, non-error message — non-error on purpose, since an isError result is exactly what provokes another retry:

This checklist task has used all 3 of its attempts. Do NOT retry it again —
either amend the plan with a different approach, or tell <owner> exactly what is blocking it.

The counters are scoped to the run, not the turn. An operator message clears them and reopens tasks the attempt guard closed with a fresh budget — narrowly, touching only blocked/failed tasks that are actually at or over budget.

Escalation is itself bounded. In guided mode the engine hands a stuck plan back to PRIME at most MAX_ESCALATIONS (3) times before giving up and asking the human: an escalation loop is still a loop.

One deliberate interaction with effort: a task on its last attempt is promoted to high effort, so the final try is not the cheapest one.
